Gunung Palung orangutans

Gunung Palung National Park, West Kalimantan, Indonesia
leaf kiss-squeak
Communication

"Kiss-squeak with leaves: Using leaves on mouth to amplify sound, then drop leaf" (van Schaik et al. 2003). Kiss-squeak on its own is considered universal at all studied orangutan sites, but use of leaves to amplify sound customary at this site, not customary at other sites.

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: "Kiss-squeak with leaves: Using leaves on mouth to amplify sound, then drop leaf" (van Schaik et al. 2003). Kiss-squeak on its own is considered universal at all studied orangutan sites, but use of leaves to amplify sound customary at this site, not customary at other sites.

Vertical: Lameira et al. note difference in function of kiss-squeak as alarm call. "unlike the kiss-squeak system at Tuanan, the two-pronged kiss-squeak system at Cabang Panti did not appear to relate to a perceived threat. Even though unhabituated individuals at Cabang Panti showed signs of disturbance in the presence of human observers (e.g. as expressed by flight and/or displays), this was not reflected in their use of leaf kiss-squeaks." They conclude possibility of social learning but not specific type

Horizontal: "Altogether, the results from this study concur with the literature suggesting that leaf kiss-squeaks may be socially learned within each population and that they represent cultural variants [3,4,23]. Future controlled experiments in captivity may assess the role of social learning in more detail."

Oblique: "Altogether, the results from this study concur with the literature suggesting that leaf kiss-squeaks may be socially learned within each population and that they represent cultural variants [3,4,23]. Future controlled experiments in captivity may assess the role of social learning in more detail."

Domains: communication

Sources: [1] [2]

Sebangau orangutans

Sebangau National Park
nesting calls
Communication

Orangutans sometimes produce a call after building their nightly nest. Calls vary among populations. In Suaq, this is described a

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: Orangutans sometimes produce a call after building their nightly nest. Calls vary among populations. In Suaq, this is described a "raspberry" call, differing from calls/lack thereof at other sites (Wich et al. 2012)

Vertical: Inferred vocal learning due to innovation of unique calls and experiments on great apes showing social learning, but unclear from research thus far.

Domains: communication

Sources: [3]

Tanjung Puting orangutans

Tanjung Puting National Park, Central Kalimantan, Borneo, Indonesia
snag-riding
Social

"Ride on pushed-over snag as it falls, then grab on to vegetation before it crashes on ground". van Schaik et al. 2003 classify as customary at this site and absent at other orangutan sites; "very likely cultural variant" (van Schaik et al. 2003)

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: "Ride on pushed-over snag as it falls, then grab on to vegetation before it crashes on ground". van Schaik et al. 2003 classify as customary at this site and absent at other orangutan sites; "very likely cultural variant" (van Schaik et al. 2003)

Vertical: described as part of display by adult males by Galdikas (1983)

Domains: social

Sources: [1] [4]

mother-infant calls
Communication

"Throat scrape" calls used by mothers to call back separated infants, distinct from calls used in Ketambe populations and from no maternal calls in other populations

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: "Throat scrape" calls used by mothers to call back separated infants, distinct from calls used in Ketambe populations and from no maternal calls in other populations

Vertical: Inferred to be at least partially due to social vocal learning as call variation was independent of genetic variation between populations, but exact mode of learning unclear

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown

Description: Orangutans sometimes produce a call after building their nightly nest. Calls vary among populations. In Tuanan, this is described a "nest smack", differing from calls/lack thereof at other sites (Wich et al. 2012)

Vertical: Inferred vocal learning due to innovation of unique calls and experiments on great apes showing social learning, but specific mode unclear for this behavior from research thus far.
